info.bio:
Manic Street Preachers es un grupo de rock procedente de Gales, Reino Unido, formado por James Dean Bradfield (voz y guitarra), Sean Moore (batería) y Nicky Wire (bajo).

La banda se formó en 1986, tomando influencia de bandas como Badfinger y Joy Division, sumándole guitarras agresivas, como un cruce a mitad camino del indie y el punk más tradicional; sus tres primeros discos se caracterizaron por letras poéticas y reivindicativas. Hasta que la misteriosa desaparición de Richey James en 1995  los reorganizó  como trío.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: "For Real" Self-Mutilation Incident (May 15, 1991)
podcast.body: After a gig at the Norwich Art Center, NME reviewer Steve LeMack questioned the band's sincerity. During a private conversation, Richie Edwards dramatically carved the words "for real" into his forearm with a razor blade, resulting in 17 stitches and significant blood loss. A photographer captured the graphic event, leading to an internal debate at the NME offices about publishing the pictures, which were eventually printed and generated considerable notoriety for the band. "I mean, who carries a razor blade with him? And he carved the words for real into his forearm. Blood gushed everywhere, but Richie insisted on talking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Apparent Suicide Attempt (July 18, 1994)
podcast.body: Richie Edwards' mental state culminated in an apparent suicide attempt when his parents found him in a bathtub, bleeding from his arms, intoxicated and drugged. He was rushed to the hospital, where he was diagnosed with severe depression and voluntarily admitted to a psychiatric hospital the following day. "He phoned his parents, who raced over to his apartment to find him lying in the bathtub with blood seeping out of his arms. He was stoned and he was drunk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Bangkok Concert Self-Harm (April 23, 1994)
podcast.body: During a concert in Bangkok, a fan sent miniature ceremonial swords backstage with a request for Richie Edwards to slash himself on stage. Richie complied, inflicting visible wounds across his chest, stating, "The fan asked me to. I didn't want to let him down." "When the band explained Bangkok on April 23, 1994, a fan sent some miniature ceremonial swords backstage with a note asking Richie to slash himself on stage. Which he did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Hamburg Incident (December 2, 1994)
podcast.body: After a show in Hamburg, Richie was found outside the band's hotel in his pajamas, repeatedly banging his head against a brick wall until he was bloody, moaning, "I want to go home." This incident led to the immediate termination of the European leg of the tour due to intense band tension. "On December 2, 1994, after a show in Hamburg, Richie was found outside the band's hotel in his pajamas, bashing his head against a brick wall until he was bloodied."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Last Appearance (December 21, 1994)
podcast.body: Richie Edwards' final public appearance with the Manic Street Preachers was at the Astoria in London, concluding a three-night stand. During this performance, he smashed his guitar at the end of the set and then used the broken remains to beat himself over the head. "Richie's last appearance with the manics was three weeks later at a gig at the Astoria in London, December 21, 1994."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Priory Hospital Stay and Diagnosis (July 28 - Sept 8, 1994)
podcast.body: Richie was transferred to the renowned Priory Hospital in London, where he was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder, a condition that explained his difficulties with identity, relationships, and detachment from reality. He was prescribed a six-week stay, a 12-step program, and the maximum dose of Prozac, while the band continued to play gigs to cover his mounting medical bills. "On July 28, 1994, he was moved to primary hospital, a renowned rehab facility in London popular with the celebrity set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Alleged Sightings and Car Discovery (February 1995)
podcast.body: On February 7, a cab driver allegedly picked Richie up from a hotel in Newport and drove him for £68 cash. About a week later, a fan reportedly spoke to him at a Newport bus station, and he was allegedly seen at a passport office. On February 14, Richie's car was found at the Aust Service Station by the Severn Bridge, a known suicide spot, with a parking ticket and reported as abandoned three days later. "On February 7, a cab driver allegedly picked him up from a hotel in the well-city of Newport and drove him around for a bit. The ride cost 68 pounds, which the passenger paid in cash. Then, a fan apparently talked to him about a week later at a bus station in the well-city of Newport. He was also allegedly seen at a passport office. Richie's car was found on February 14 that the nearby Austin Service Station by the Severin Bridge, which is supposedly a favorite spot for those seeking suicide. It had gotten a ticket for illegal parking. Three days later, it was reported as abandoned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rock's Most Mysterious Musicians

podcast.title: Disappearance Details (February 1, 1995)
podcast.body: At 7 AM on February 1, 1995, Richie checked out of the hotel and drove his Vauxhall Cavalier to his home in Cardiff, Wales, where he left belongings, including his Prozac bottle and passport, on his desk. Over the previous two weeks, he had withdrawn £200 daily, totaling £2800, for unknown purposes, possibly for the US tour or a new desk he had seen in Cardiff. "At 7am on February 1, 1995, Richie checked out of the hotel and drove his voxol cabalier to his home in Cardiff Wales, where he dropped off some stuff, including his bottle of Prozac. And he also left his passport, which he left right on the desk. As for money, well, for the past two weeks, Richie had been withdrawing 200 pounds a day from his bank account, taking out a total of 2800 pounds. What was he using that money for? No idea. It could have been for the US tour, although he talked about buying a new desk for his home. He'd found it in a shop in Cardiff, but he never bought it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rock's Most Mysterious Musicians

podcast.title: Disappearance from Embassy Hotel (January 31 - February 1, 1995)
podcast.body: After a final rehearsal with the band on January 31, 1995, Richie gave small presents to his bandmates, possibly as an apology. He then checked into the Embassy Hotel in London with James Dean Bradfield. Richie was last seen by James Dean Bradfield at approximately 8:30 pm on January 31, 1995, in his room (516), taking a bath and stating he would spend a quiet night alone, before he vanished completely by February 1, 1995. "James Dean Bradfield may have been the last person to see Richie alive. This brings us to February 1, 1995. What happened? Well, we'll explore that next."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Last Known Contact (January 31, 1995)
podcast.body: At 8:30 PM on January 31, James Dean Bradfield knocked on Richie's door, room 561, but Richie politely declined to go out, stating he was about to take a bath. He later called his mother, expressing reservations about the upcoming trip to America but acknowledging it as a necessary part of being in a rock band; this was the last time anyone heard from him. "At 8.30 that night, James knocked on Richie's door, room 561, and asked if he wanted to go out. Richie politely declined, saying that he was just about to have a bath. He later called his mother to say that he wasn't wild about having to go to America, but at the same time, he understood it was something people and rock bands have to do from time to time. And that was the last anyone heard from him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Disappearance Behavior (January 1995)
podcast.body: After his dog's death, Richie shaved off all his hair and began acting even more strangely than usual, despite being off alcohol and drugs. On January 31, he and bandmate James Dean Bradfield checked into the London Embassy Hotel in preparation for a North American promotional trip. "After that, Richie shaved off all his hair and began acting even more strangely than usual, even though he was off alcohol and drugs at that point. On January 31, he and bandmate James Dean Bradford checked into the London Embassy Hotel on Bayes Water Road, which is right across the street from High Park in London. The purpose was to get ready for a promotional trip through North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rock's Most Mysterious Musicians

podcast.title: Richie Edwards' Disappearance (1995)
podcast.body: Richie Edwards, an extreme member of the Manic Street Preachers known for depression, anorexia, drug use, and self-mutilation, disappeared on February 1, 1995, following the death of his dog on January 14, 1995. On January 31, 1995, he checked into a London hotel with James Dean Bradfield, declined to go out, and later called his mom expressing reluctance about an upcoming North American promo tour; he checked out at 7 AM on February 1st, drove to his Cardiff, Wales home to drop off Prozac and his passport, and his car was found 12 days later by a country bridge with a dead battery. No body, clues, or motives were ever found, leading to his legal declaration of death on February 1, 2002, though "Elvis-like sightings" continued in various locations. "What happened to Richie Edwards on February 1st, 1995?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Declared Legally Dead (2008)
podcast.body: On November 23, 2008, Richie was legally declared dead by his family, who assumed he had taken his own life at the age of 27, though his fate remains officially unknown. "On November 23, 2008, Richie was declared legally dead by his family, having assumed to have taken his own life at that magical and doomed age of, yes, 27. But the bottom line is, nobody knows for sure."

podcast.title: Band Slogan
podcast.body: The band, with Richie Edwards' involvement, developed their distinctive slogan: "culture, alienation, boredom, and despair." This slogan reflected their intellectual and critical approach to society and music. "It was with Richie that the Manics came up with their slogan, culture, alienation, boredom, and despair."

podcast.title: Car Evidence and Discrepancies
podcast.body: The car's dead battery suggested it had been running the radio or heater for extended periods, and a receipt for 30 pence indicated he crossed the Severn Bridge at 2:55 AM on February 1, which conflicted with his 7 AM London hotel checkout. The car also showed signs that someone had been living in it for at least a couple of nights. "The battery was dead, suggesting that Richie had been running the radio or the heater for long periods of time without turning the engine on. There was a receipt and 30 pence in change, showing that he recently crossed the bridge at 2.55 am on February 1. But that didn't make any sense, since he reportedly checked out of his London hotel room at 7 that morning. And it looked like someone had been living in the car for at least a couple of nights."

podcast.title: Columbia Records Signing After "For Real" Incident
podcast.body: Six days after the highly publicized "for real" self-mutilation incident, Columbia Records signed the band. This suggests that the controversy and notoriety surrounding Richie Edwards significantly contributed to attracting major label attention. "Six days after he carved himself up in Norwich, Columbia records signed the band and allowed them to create an 18-track 73-minute album entitled Generation Terrorists."

podcast.title: DNA Test and Other Theories
podcast.body: In early 2002, human feet found downstream from the Severn Bridge were conclusively proven not to be Richie's via DNA. Other theories suggested he died in the 2004 Phuket tsunami, disappeared to Israel, or followed his uncle's pattern of disappearing for a decade, a story Richie was reportedly fascinated by. "In early 2002, a pair of human feet was discovered downstream from that Severin Bridge, but DNA results proved conclusively that this wasn't Richie, or even part of Richie. Richie was the theory that he ended up in Puket, Thailand, and died in the 2004 tsunami. Still another theory says that he disappeared to Israel. Another theory is that he took after his uncle, who once disappeared for 10 years before showing up again. Richie was apparently fascinated by that story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Delayed Recognition
podcast.body: Similar to My Bloody Valentine and Dinosaur Jr., the Manic Street Preachers experienced a delayed recognition, not truly breaking through until later, reflecting the challenges faced by Shoegaze bands in gaining immediate industry support. "algo muy parecido les acabaría pasando a otras bandas como los Manic Street Richard, o como Dinosaur Junior."

podcast.title: Downward Spiral and Dog's Death
podcast.body: Despite therapy and support, Richie was in an unstoppable downward spiral, with the death of his dog on January 14, 1995, appearing to be the final trigger. "But despite several attempts at therapy and rehab and all kinds of support from his bandmates and friends, it was obvious that Richie was in an unstoppable downward spiral. The final trigger seemed to have been the death of his dog on January 14, 1995."

podcast.title: Early Guitar-Driven Sound
podcast.body: In their initial stages, the band exhibited a more guitar-driven sound, which placed them in the shoegaze vein and drew influences from The Jesus and Mary Chain. "los maneguester preachers en sus inicios, que hacían como un sesonido más guitarrero, más en la vertende de Jesus and Mary Chain."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Final Days Before Disappearance
podcast.body: Following the holiday season, Richie ceased writing in his diary on January 17, 1995, just three days after his beloved cocker spaniel, Snoopy, died at age 17, leaving him inconsolable. Coupled with band tensions and a relationship breakdown, he seemed to be on the verge of a crisis. He made four trips to a Cardiff bank machine, withdrawing £200 each time, spending money on mundane items like comic books, books, VHS movies, and flowers for his mother, whom he visited one last time. "By the end of January, Richie was teetering on the edge of something really, really bad. He also seemed to be up to something."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Growing Rift and Paranoia
podcast.body: Following the Bangkok trip, a rift began to form between Richie and the rest of the band, marked by his increasing paranoia, as evidenced by his insistence on sitting alone at the back of the plane. He also began to identify with Pink, the burned-out rock star character from Pink Floyd's *The Wall*. "The trip to Thailand also seemed to mark the beginning of a rift with the rest of the band. Flying to and from Bangkok, Richie insisted on sitting at the back of the plane by himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lack of Clues and Theories
podcast.body: Despite extensive searches, no body, clues, or motives were ever found for Richie's disappearance. Theories include Elvis-like sightings in Goa, India, the Canary Islands, London, and Africa. "But that was it. It was gone. There was no body. There were no clues. And worst of all, no motives. Why did Richie choose to disappear so completely? Since then, there have been Elvis-like sightings of Richie in Goa, India, in the Canary Islands, in London, in Africa."

podcast.title: On the Brink of Massive Success
podcast.body: Towards the end of 1994 and the beginning of 1995, the Manic Street Preachers were "on the verge of becoming absolutely massive" and recognized for having "a ton of potential." They were also a favored subject for journalists. "The Manic Street preachers were on the verge of becoming absolutely massive at the end of 1994 in the beginning of 1995."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin and Early Life in Blackwood
podcast.body: All members of the Manic Street Preachers originated from Blackwood, a "south and bleak coal town" in South Wales, which had been abandoned by industry, leaving behind only betting shops and pubs. Richie Edwards described the environment as one of "unemployment, violence, and defeatism." "Like all members of the Manic Street Preachers, Richie was from South Wales, a south and bleak coal town called Blackwood, abandoned by industry, and leaving nothing but betting shops and pubs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Post-Disappearance Regrouping and Success
podcast.body: After Richey Edwards' disappearance, the band successfully "regrouped" and went on to become "one of the most successful bands they ever come out of Wales," selling millions of albums and concert tickets globally. "Now they were able to regroup and turn themselves into one of the most successful bands they ever come out of Wales, selling millions of albums and concert tickets around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Post-Rehab Fragility and Relapse
podcast.body: Upon discharge from Priory Hospital on September 8, 1994, Richie was back on the road with the band two weeks later, but remained extremely fragile, cycling between hope and hopelessness. He maintained an unhealthy regimen of smoking 65 cigarettes a day, consuming 30 cups of coffee, and drinking half a bottle of vodka daily to cope. "He was better, but still very emotionally fragile, veering from hopefulness to hopelessness. He was smoking 65 cigarettes a day and powering himself with 30 cups of coffee to counteract the half bottle of vodka he habitually drank."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Richie Edwards' Disturbances
podcast.body: Richie Edwards was described as the most extreme member of Manic Street Preachers, suffering from depression, anorexia, drug use, and bouts of self-mutilation, and was morbidly fascinated with Kurt Cobain's final days. "Richie was the most extreme member of the Manic Street Preachers. He was also quite disturbed and prone to depression and erexia, drug use and boats of self-mutilation. He was also morbidly fascinated with the last days of Kurt Cobain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rock's Most Mysterious Musicians

podcast.title: Richie Edwards' Role as "Minister of Propaganda"
podcast.body: In the spring of 1989, Richie Edwards was adopted as the fourth member and spokesman for the band, referred to as their "Minister of Propaganda." Despite having "zero musical ability" and mostly miming on stage with his amp turned down, his primary role was to attract attention, write lyrics, and contribute intellectually to the band's image and sound. "In the spring of 1989, the Manic Street Preachers adopted Richie as a fourth member of the band and spokesman. He was referred to as their Minister of Propaganda."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Richie's Declining Mental and Physical Health
podcast.body: As the band's career took off, Richie's personal struggles intensified, marked by insomnia, alcohol abuse leading to rehab, and increasing isolation. His weight plummeted, and his self-harm escalated, including slashing his chest in Amsterdam and using a meat cleaver (allegedly to avoid performing) and cutting himself on stage in Bangkok. "Even as the manic's career started to take off, things were not good for Richie. He had always suffered from insomnia and used alcohol to get to sleep. That resulted in a trip to rehab."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards

podcast.title: Unique Rock and Roll Philosophy
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, the Manics distinguished themselves by professing to have more in common with American hard rock bands like Guns N' Roses and Motley Crue than with bands from Manchester or the emerging Britpop scene. They openly bragged about wanting to sell millions of records, a desire uncommon among indie bands of that era, and readily signed with a major label. "The Manics were different for the early 1990s. They professed to have more in common with guns and roses in Motley Crew than anything from Manchester or early Britpop, saying that real rock and roll came from America."

xref.title: Intellectual and Literary Figure
xref.body: Richie was the intellectual force behind the Manic Street Preachers, well-versed in figures like Karl Marx, Albert Camus, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerouac, and Joseph Conrad, as well as the Beat Poets. He meticulously rehearsed philosophical and literary quotes for interviews, solidifying his role as the band's literary expert. "Richie knew about Karl Marx, Albert Kamu, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerawak, Joseph Conrad, and all the beat poets."

xref.title: Manic Street Preachers' Self-Comparison
xref.body: The Manic Street Preachers openly stated they felt they had more in common with bands like Guns N' Roses than with the emerging Britpop or Manchester music scene of the early 1990s. This reflected their preference for a more aggressive, American-style rock and roll. "They professed to have more in common with guns and roses in Motley Crew than anything from Manchester or early Britpop, saying that real rock and roll came from America."
